section.title: The Lord Is My Light and My Salvation
section.sectionRationale: A psalm of David that moves from confident trust, verses 1-6, into urgent lament and plea, verses 7-13, before closing with an exhortation to wait on the LORD. Its turn from bold confidence to desperate prayer, and back to hope, models the honest rhythm of real faith under real pressure.
section.thesis: David's confidence that the LORD is his light and salvation does not remove his fear and need, but drives him to seek God's face all the more urgently, resting his hope on the certainty that he will see God's goodness in the land of the living.
section.frameNote: Four movements: confident trust that the LORD is light and salvation (1-3); the one thing asked, to dwell in God's house and be exalted above enemies (4-6); an urgent cry for mercy and God's presence despite even parental abandonment (7-10); and a prayer for guidance from false witnesses, closing in confident hope and exhortation (11-14).

units.label: The LORD is my light and my salvation

verses.text: The LORD is my {{or|light}} and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life, whom shall I dread?
When the wicked came upon me to devour my flesh, my enemies and foes stumbled and fell.
Though an army encamps around me, my heart will not fear; though a war breaks out against me, I will keep my trust.

units.label: One thing I have asked of the LORD

verses.text: One thing I have asked of the LORD; this is what I desire: to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze on the beauty of the LORD and seek Him in His temple.
For in the day of trouble He will hide me in His shelter; He will conceal me under the cover of His tent; He will set me high upon a rock.
Then my head will be held high above my enemies around me. At His tabernacle I will offer sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make music to the LORD.

units.label: Hide not Your face from me

verses.text: Hear, O LORD, my voice when I call; be merciful and answer me.
My heart said, "Seek His face." Your face, O LORD, I will {{baqash|seek}}.

Hide not Your face from me, nor turn away Your servant in anger. You have been my helper; do not leave me or forsake me, 
O God of my salvation.
Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me.

Teach me Your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path, 
because of my oppressors.

Do not hand me over to the will of my foes, for false witnesses rise up against me, 
breathing out violence.

Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD 
in the land of the living.

Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and {{chazaq|courageous}}. 
Wait patiently for the LORD!

or.gloss: Light, the first thing God spoke into being, Genesis 1:3, and a common picture of God's saving presence dispelling darkness, danger, and fear. David names the LORD Himself as his light, not merely a giver of light.

baqash.gloss: To seek, search for, desire earnestly. David's whole heart echoes God's own invitation back to Him, turning command into desire, 'Seek His face,' answered by 'Your face, O LORD, I will seek.'

chazaq.gloss: To be strong, firm, courageous, often used in commands to take heart before a daunting task, as with Joshua, Joshua 1:6-9. The psalm's closing exhortation urges this same strengthened resolve while waiting on the LORD.

basic.context: David opens with bold confidence, the LORD as his light and salvation, whom he need not fear even facing an army. But by verse 7 the tone shifts into urgent plea, asking God not to hide His face, not to forsake him, even if his own parents were to abandon him. The psalm closes by returning to confident hope, that David will see God's goodness in the land of the living, and a call to wait patiently and courageously on the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's shift from bold confidence to desperate lament and back again should be read not as contradiction but as the honest shape of real faith, which does not pretend fear away but brings it directly to God, anchored in His character rather than in the absence of danger.
basic.originalLanguages: David calls the LORD his or, light, not merely a source of light but light itself. His deepest desire, baqash, to seek God's face, answers God's own invitation, and the psalm closes urging chazaq, strength and courage, while waiting on the LORD rather than looking to circumstances for confidence.
basic.typology: David's one request, to dwell in the house of the LORD and gaze on His beauty, verse 4, anticipates the greater and permanent dwelling Christ provides for His people in His Father's house, John 14:2-3. His hope in verse 10, that the LORD receives him even if father and mother forsake him, anticipates the full adoption believers receive in Christ, Romans 8:15.
basic.christ: Jesus is the true light, John 8:12, of whom David's confession is a shadow, and the one who grants not merely a visit to God's house but a permanent, prepared place there, John 14:2-3. Where David could only ask to seek God's face, believers now behold the glory of God fully in the face of Jesus Christ, 2 Corinthians 4:6. And David's confidence that the LORD receives him even if parents forsake him is fulfilled in the full adoption as sons and daughters that comes through Christ, Romans 8:15, Ephesians 1:5.
basic.god: God is shown as both refuge and answer to fear, one whose presence, not the absence of enemies or danger, is the true security, and one who receives the abandoned and forsaken even when the closest human relationships fail.
basic.crossReferences: John 8:12 shows Jesus as the light of the world, fulfilling David's confession of the LORD as his light. John 14:2-3 shows Christ preparing a permanent place in His Father's house, the fulfillment of David's one request in verse 4. Romans 8:15 shows believers receiving the Spirit of adoption, sons and daughters, whom no earthly abandonment can undo.
basic.oneStory: David's confidence that the LORD is his light and salvation carries him through fear, betrayal, and even the possibility of parental abandonment, into a settled hope of seeing God's goodness. That hope is fulfilled completely in Jesus Christ, the true light of the world, who receives the forsaken as adopted children and prepares an everlasting place for them in His Father's house.

context.literary:
The two halves of Psalm 27 differ in grammar as well as mood. Verses 1 to 6 speak about God in the third person: the LORD is my light, the LORD is the stronghold of my life. From verse 7 David turns and speaks to God in the second person, 'Hear, O LORD, my voice', and he keeps that address to the end of verse 12. Then in verse 13 he steps back into a statement of confidence, and verse 14 turns outward to a listener with a command, 'Wait patiently for the LORD.' The psalm therefore moves from testimony, to prayer, to exhortation, and the last line is aimed at the reader.

Verse 4 is the hinge of the entire poem. It opens with 'One thing', it is the longest sentence in the psalm, and it is the only place where David names what he wants above everything else. Its three infinitives are 'to dwell', 'to gaze' and 'to seek', so the desire is for a home, a vision and a conversation. Verses 5 and 6 then say what the dwelling will do for him: shelter in trouble, a rock beneath, a lifted head, and shouts of joy at the tent.

The enemy vocabulary rises and falls. The wicked 'stumbled and fell' in verse 2, an army encamps in verse 3, oppressors and false witnesses appear in verses 11 and 12, and yet the section of praise in verse 6 already sees the head lifted above them. The psalm names 'my heart' at the centre of both halves, verses 3 and 8, and turns it toward the reader at the close, verse 14, so that the heart is the battlefield where fear is fought and courage is given.

The pairing of 'wait' in verse 14 is deliberate: the command appears twice, framing the last line with the same verb, so that the poem ends on a rhythm of patience rather than a sudden resolution. The psalm ends with the enemy still around and the hope still ahead.
context.historical:
Tradition puts the psalm in David's hand, and the title of the psalm in the Hebrew text says so. The situations it describes fit more than one episode of his life: the pursuit by Saul, the flight from Absalom, or the seasons of open war. The psalm names no particular event, and it may have been kept for a range of circumstances. What it does show is the world of a king who lived under threat from armies, courts and false witnesses.

The 'house of the LORD' and 'temple' of verse 4 create a puzzle for a Davidic setting, since the temple was not built until Solomon. The Hebrew word for temple, hekal, is used of the sanctuary at Shiloh in the days of Eli, 1 Samuel 1:9 and 3:3, and verse 6 speaks of a 'tabernacle', a tent, so David may be describing the tent he pitched for the ark, or the old sanctuary at Gibeon, or he may be speaking in the broad terms of the sanctuary as the place of God's presence. The desire is not for a building but for the presence that dwells there.

Verse 10 has a hard edge in that world. To be abandoned by father and mother was to lose the people who guaranteed protection and inheritance. Without a family there was no one to redeem property, avenge a wrong or speak in court. David's boast that the LORD will 'receive' him means that God will do what a family did, and the point is sharpened by the strife in David's own household, 2 Samuel 15:13, when David fled his own son.

Verse 12 mentions false witnesses. In Israel a person could be executed on the word of two or three witnesses, Deuteronomy 19:15, so a false witness was lethal. The psalm places that fear beside the confidence of verse 1, and it shows how much depended on a God who saw beyond the testimony of men. In later Jewish practice the psalm came to be recited during the season leading up to the autumn festivals, a use that shows how easily it was heard as a prayer for the whole community and not only for one king.
context.canonical:
Psalm 27 draws on many strands of the Old Testament and is quoted in many later prayers. The confession 'The LORD is my light' has an echo in Micah 7:8, where a person sitting in darkness says the LORD will be his light, and in Isaiah 60:19 to 20, where the LORD becomes the everlasting light of His people and the days of sorrow cease. Psalm 36:9 says, 'in Your light we see light,' which reads like a commentary on the first verse.

The desire for the house of God runs through the Psalter. The sons of Korah say one day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere, Psalm 84:10, David says he has beheld God's power and glory in the sanctuary, Psalm 63:2, and the whole collection of pilgrim songs longs for Zion. Verse 4 sums up all of it in the phrase 'one thing'. The seeking of God's face is bound to the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25 to 26, in which the LORD's face shines and He gives peace, and Psalm 4:6 asks for that same shining.

The exhortation of the close, 'be strong and courageous', is the language of Joshua's commissioning, Deuteronomy 31:6 and Joshua 1:9, and it turns up again in Psalm 31:24. The word 'wait' is the theme of Isaiah 40:31, where those who wait on the LORD renew their strength.

In the New Testament Jesus takes the title of light for Himself, John 8:12, and the apostle calls Him the one in whom 'there is no darkness at all', 1 John 1:5. The face of God that David sought is seen 'in the face of Jesus Christ', 2 Corinthians 4:6, and the pure in heart 'will see God', Matthew 5:8. At the end of the Bible, the city has no need of sun or moon because the glory of God gives it light, Revelation 21:23, and 'They will see His face', Revelation 22:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wants his hearers to learn how fear and faith actually live together. He does not tell them that a believer never feels dread. He models a man who says 'whom shall I fear?' in verse 1 and then, six verses later, begs God not to hide His face. The first hearers were meant to notice that the confidence of the opening was not shallow, because it sits beside a plain admission that the danger was real.

He wants them to know what the believer asks for first. Of all the things a king might want, David names one: to be where God is, to look at Him and to talk with Him. The rest of the psalm shows why: God's presence is shelter, height and joy. That priority is an instruction for any worshipper who is tempted to treat the sanctuary as a means to a good outcome rather than the goal itself.

He also means to show a habit of talking to yourself in the presence of God. Verse 8 records the heart speaking and the prayer answering it. Verse 14 addresses the listener with the same words the heart needed. The instruction to 'wait' comes from a man who has been waiting and is not yet finished. He does not promise quick relief; he promises that the goodness of the LORD will be seen 'in the land of the living', and he asks his hearers to hold on until then.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's experience and his prayer, and its most direct instructions are the last two lines: wait for the LORD and be strong. Those are commands, and they are given to the reader. The rest is testimony that shapes how we pray without being a set of promises that every enemy will stumble, as they did in verse 2. The believer who reads that verse as a guarantee of victory over every opponent will be disappointed; the New Testament itself records that faithful people were killed, Hebrews 11:36 to 38.

The desire to dwell in the house of the LORD is also not a command to move into a building. In David's day the tent was the place where God had promised to meet His people. In the New Testament the church is a dwelling for God, Ephesians 2:21 to 22, and the believer's body is a temple, 1 Corinthians 6:19. The application is not to spend all our time in a place of worship but to keep first the thing that the place stood for, the presence of God.

Finally, verse 10 records David's confidence that God will receive him even if his parents abandon him. It is not a rebuke of parents, and it does not tell a person to leave a family. It is a promise to those who have been left, and a caution to the rest of us about how much rests on those who care for the vulnerable, Psalm 68:5.

debates.question: Is Psalm 27 one psalm, or two poems joined together?

views.label: One psalm that follows the rhythm of real faith
views.case: Verse 6 ends with sacrifices and songs, and verse 7 begins with a cry to be heard. It is common in the Psalter for trust and lament to sit in one prayer, and the same three words, 'my heart', bind the parts together. The phrase 'wait patiently' at the close also answers the fear that is voiced in the middle.

views.label: Two originally separate compositions, a song of trust and a prayer of lament
views.case: The change of address and mood at verse 7 is abrupt, and some scholars suggest that an older song of confidence was joined to a lament, perhaps for use in a liturgy. Verses 1 to 6 speak about God and verses 7 to 12 speak to Him, and the two have different vocabulary for enemies.

views.label: One psalm written in a time of crisis, reading the confidence as a response to the fear
views.case: Trust here is not the opposite of fear; it is the stance a person takes in order to face it. The first section may then be read as the confession that David made to himself and the second as the prayer that followed when it was tested.

debates.bearing: The canonical form is what the church has always prayed. Whatever its history, the psalm teaches that boldness and begging are not competitors, and that the one who says 'whom shall I fear?' can also say 'do not leave me.'

debates.question: How should verse 13 be read: 'Still I am certain to see' or 'I would have despaired unless I believed'?

views.label: A statement of settled confidence
views.case: This is how the BSB and most modern translations take it: 'Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.' It matches the confident closing of verse 14 and the boldness of verse 1.

views.label: An unfinished sentence: 'Unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living...'
views.case: The Hebrew begins with the word lule, 'if not', and the sentence trails off. The Hebrew scribes marked the word with dots above it, and the ancient Greek translation reads it as 'I believe to see', while English versions of an older era completed the thought with 'I had fainted, unless I had believed'. The broken sentence would express the depth of the alternative, too terrible to speak.

debates.bearing: Both readings arrive at the same place: David's hope in seeing God's goodness is what carries him. The broken form of the Hebrew, if intended, shows that his faith is not a comfortable certainty but an insistence made at the edge of despair.

debates.question: What is the 'temple' or 'house' David wishes to dwell in, if the temple had not yet been built?

views.label: The tent sanctuary in David's day
views.case: The Hebrew hekal was used of the sanctuary at Shiloh, 1 Samuel 3:3, and verse 6 uses the word for a tent. David pitched a tent for the ark in Jerusalem, and he could have called it the house of the LORD.

views.label: A later addition or later setting
views.case: Others argue that the language points to Solomon's temple and that the psalm was shaped in the temple period, so that a Davidic prayer was adapted for the later sanctuary, like the other 'of David' psalms that speak of the temple.

views.label: A figure for the presence of God
views.case: Because the prayer is to gaze on God's beauty and seek Him, the house is a poetic way of naming His presence, and no particular building is in view.

debates.bearing: The bearing on how we read the psalm is small. In all three views the desire is for God, not for the structure, and the language of the psalm was later carried unchanged into the Christian understanding of the church and the heavenly city.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse holds two words that are easy to pass over. 'My salvation' is yeshu'ati from the root yasha, whose basic sense is to make roomy or to bring out of a tight place. Salvation in the Old Testament begins as release from being hemmed in. The word for 'stronghold' is ma'oz, a fortress or refuge, and it is set beside 'the LORD is my light', so the verse names three pictures: light against darkness, room against pressure, walls against attack. The 'stronghold of my life' is chayyay, the life itself, so the LORD is the fortress in which David's entire existence is kept.

In verse 4 the phrase 'One thing' is achat, and the verb 'I have asked' is shaal, the ordinary word for asking. It is the verb of a petitioner, not of a person taking. The wish 'to gaze' uses chazah, to see with attention, the verb of a visionary; Psalm 11:7 says the upright 'will see His face'. What is seen is God's no'am, 'beauty', a word for pleasantness or delight, as when Psalm 90:17 asks that the favour of the Lord rest on us and Proverbs 3:17 says wisdom's ways are pleasant. The beauty of the LORD is not a matter of looks but of the sweetness of His character.

In verse 5 the word 'shelter' is sukkah, a booth, the leafy hut of the Feast of Tabernacles, and the second line says He will 'conceal me' with a related word, seter, the secret place. The lines together suggest a woven shelter and a hidden interior. Psalm 31:20 uses the same pair of words for the hiding of God's people from the plots of men.

The word 'receive' in verse 10 is asaf, 'to gather in', the verb used when a lost animal is brought home to the house, Deuteronomy 22:2. The picture is of the LORD taking in the one whom parents have cast out.

In verse 13 the small word lule opens the sentence, and it is written with dots above it in the Hebrew text, a scribal mark drawing attention to it. The BSB's 'Still I am certain' smooths what is really a broken sentence, 'If I had not believed...'. In the final verse 'wait' is qavah, a verb that comes from the language of stretching a cord and so means to wait with tension and expectation, the root behind the Hebrew word for hope, and it is the verb of Isaiah 40:31. The second command in the line, the 'courageous' verb, is amats, paired with 'strong' in Deuteronomy 31:6 and Joshua 1:9.

typology.type: The one thing: dwelling in the house of the LORD, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: David asks for a permanent place in God's presence, and the Old Testament tent gave him only a visit. Jesus says, 'In My Father's house are many rooms,' John 14:2 to 3, and promises to prepare a place and welcome His people to be where He is. The believer is already called a member of God's household, Ephesians 2:19, and the church is a dwelling for God in the Spirit, Ephesians 2:22. The type falls short in that David could only go to a location; in Christ the dwelling is a relationship with a Person and, in the end, with the new creation.

typology.type: The shelter, tent and rock, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: The LORD hides David in His shelter, conceals him in His tent, and sets him on a rock. The same three pictures are drawn into the New Testament with a fresh centre. Christ is the rock, 1 Corinthians 10:4, and those who trust in Him are hidden with Him in God, Colossians 3:3. The shelter of Revelation 7:15 is the very tent of God spread over the multitude that came out of the great tribulation. The type is partial because David's rock kept him safe in danger, whereas Christ brings his people through death.

typology.type: Seeing the beauty of the LORD, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: Moses was told that no one can see God's face and live, Exodus 33:20, and David longs to gaze on the beauty of the LORD. Paul says that the glory of God is now seen 'in the face of Jesus Christ', 2 Corinthians 4:6, and Jesus tells Philip that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father, John 14:9. The fullest fulfilment is still ahead, when 'we shall see face to face', 1 Corinthians 13:12, and 'They will see His face', Revelation 22:4. The type falls short because David's gazing was in a sanctuary and in part; the promise is of an unclouded sight.

typology.type: Forsaken by father and mother, taken in by the LORD, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: David's confidence rests on a God who gathers the abandoned. The shape of it appears in the life of Christ, who was forsaken by His own disciples, Mark 14:50, and who on the cross cried out to a Father who seemed far away, Mark 15:34, so that those who are abandoned would be received. Through Him believers receive the Spirit of sonship, Romans 8:15, and are adopted into God's family, Ephesians 1:5. The type falls short because David was received in a promise, whereas believers are received in a finished work.

study.christ:
David's opening confession is fulfilled in Christ by way of the light. When Jesus says 'I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life,' John 8:12, He speaks with a claim that only the LORD Himself could make in Psalm 27:1. John calls Him the true light who gives light to everyone, John 1:9, and Paul says that the light that shone out of darkness has shone in our hearts 'in the face of Jesus Christ', 2 Corinthians 4:6. The salvation of the same verse is His name, since the name Jesus carries the sense of the LORD saves, Matthew 1:21.

The one thing that David asked is fulfilled in a Person. He wanted to gaze on the beauty of the LORD, and the Word became flesh so that people could see His glory, John 1:14. On the last night Jesus tells the disciples that He is going to prepare a place so that they may be with Him, John 14:2 to 3, which is the answer to the request to dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of one's life. Christ also prays that His people would be with Him to see His glory, John 17:24.

He fulfils the psalm as the one who was truly forsaken. Verse 10 is a promise that the LORD receives those who are left, and the cross is the place where the promise was paid for. Jesus was deserted by the Twelve and cried out that God had forsaken Him, Mark 15:34, so that it could never be truly said of a believer that God has left him. Hebrews takes up the Old Testament words 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' and gives them to the church, Hebrews 13:5.

He also lives the last verse. Waiting patiently with courage is what He did in Gethsemane, where He faced the plots of false witnesses, Matthew 26:60, and the enemies who breathed out violence, and prayed, 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. On the third day God raised Him and exalted Him to the right hand, Acts 2:32 to 33, and so the head that David saw lifted above his enemies is His first. The 'land of the living' is where He was raised.

The psalm should not be forced into a code where every image points to Christ. The enemies who devour flesh, the army and the tent are not each a pointer to Jesus. The links that the New Testament itself draws are the light, the face, the dwelling and the receiving of the abandoned, and those are enough to show that the person David longed for is the one who has come.
study.god:
Psalm 27 shows a God whose presence is the answer to fear, and it does so by naming three roles at once: light, salvation and stronghold. Each answers a different threat. Light answers the dark that hides danger, salvation answers the pressure of enemies, and the stronghold answers the assault. The question 'whom shall I fear?' is asked not because there is nothing to fear but because the one who stands behind David is greater than the fear.

He is a God who hides His face and is sought. The plea 'Hide not Your face from me,' verse 9, presupposes that God's face can be turned away, and the whole psalm has the tension between a God who is near and a God who can seem absent. Yet the seeking is answered, since verse 8 has the heart saying 'Seek His face' and David answers 'Your face, O LORD, I will seek.' God's own invitation stirs up the hunger that He then satisfies. This is a doctrine of grace: the desire to seek is itself a gift.

He is a God who teaches and leads. The prayer of verse 11, 'Teach me Your way,' asks for direction, and the request for a 'level path' shows that God's guidance is meant to make life safe, not only pious. God is not only refuge but also the one who instructs the person who takes refuge.

He is a God who receives the abandoned. The comparison with a father and mother is a bold one. God is not merely like a parent, He does what parents are supposed to do when they fail, and the same idea rings through Isaiah 49:15, where He says a mother may forget her nursing child but He will not forget His people. This is a picture of tenderness that sits inside the strong language of fortress and army.

He is a God who calls for patience. The last verse asks the believer to wait, and that shows that God's timing is not ours. The promise to see His goodness 'in the land of the living', verse 13, shows that His goodness is not only for the afterlife but for the present world, and that we wait for it in trust.

For worship, the psalm asks us to have one thing at the centre. The rest of our prayers, our fears and our plans hang from it, and the one thing is to be with God and to look at Him.

crossReferences.note: 'Though I sit in darkness, the LORD will be my light.' The prophet speaks the confession of Psalm 27:1 in the middle of ruin, showing that the claim to have the LORD as light was carried from David into the worst days of Israel's history and still held.

The LORD will be an everlasting light and the days of sorrow will cease. Psalm 27:1 speaks of the LORD as light in the present, and Isaiah projects the same light into the future when the sun and moon are no longer needed.

'For with You is the fountain of life; in Your light we see light.' It reads like a comment on Psalm 27:1: the LORD does not only shine on the believer but is the light by which the believer can see anything at all.

One day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. The sons of Korah carry the 'one thing' of Psalm 27:4 in their own words, and show that the longing for the sanctuary was a shared, national and personal love of the presence of God.

The priestly blessing asks that the LORD cause His face to shine and give peace. Psalm 27:8 to 9 depends on that promise: when David seeks God's face and prays that it not be hidden, he is asking for the blessing that Israel heard every time it was pronounced.

A mother may forget her nursing child, but the LORD will not forget. It is the nearest parallel to Psalm 27:10, and it shows that the promise of being received when parents fail belongs to the LORD's habit, not to a single poetic exaggeration.

The LORD hides His people in the secret place of His presence and conceals them in His shelter. The words are close to Psalm 27:5, and the pairing shows that the language of hiding belongs to a family of prayers in which the LORD's presence itself is the refuge.

'Be strong and courageous... He will never leave you nor forsake you.' The last line of Psalm 27 borrows Moses' words to Israel and Joshua, and the earlier plea, 'do not leave me or forsake me,' verse 9, is the same promise turned into a prayer.

Those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength. The verb 'wait' of Psalm 27:14 is the verb of this promise, and it shows what the waiting produces: the strength that David is told to have is received in the act of waiting.

'I am the light of the world.' Jesus makes the confession of Psalm 27:1 about Himself, and in doing so He places Himself in the position of the LORD, which is why the claim was found either scandalous or saving by those who heard it.

God has made His light shine in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. The face David sought is now seen, and the psalm's search finds its end in the gospel.
'They will see His face.' The gazing of Psalm 27:4 is finally granted in the new Jerusalem, and the restriction of Exodus 33:20 is lifted for a people who have been made pure in heart, Matthew 5:8.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 27 belongs to the long story of the human heart's homesickness. In the garden the man and the woman heard the sound of the LORD walking and hid from His face, Genesis 3:8, and the story of Scripture is the story of how people who fled the presence of God come back to seek it. David's 'one thing' is what the first humans lost, and the psalm shows that the loss can be reversed, though not at once.

The story that surrounds the psalm gives it its shape. The face of God is the heart of the Aaronic blessing, Numbers 6:25 to 26, and the seeking of God's face is the mark of the faithful in every age. In Psalm 27 the request is made from within a sanctuary of tents. In the prophets, God's people lose the sanctuary and the sight, and the psalm becomes a prayer for exiles, sitting in darkness and saying the LORD is their light, Micah 7:8. When Israel is scattered it is the promise of verse 10 that holds them.

The story turns in Christ. He is the light of the world, John 8:12, He is the glory seen in flesh, John 1:14, and He prepares a place in His Father's house, John 14:2 to 3. The forsaken one who cried out on the cross secured the reception of every person who trusts Him. The Spirit who cries 'Abba, Father' in the hearts of believers, Romans 8:15, gives them what the psalm only hoped for: a sense of being received, not by a stranger but by a Father.

The church still waits. Its posture is the posture of the last verse: strong, courageous and patient, living in the land of the living while the goodness of the LORD is seen in part. The end of the story is the answer to the psalm in full. In the new Jerusalem there is no temple, and there is no sun or moon, because the glory of God gives it light and the Lamb is its lamp, Revelation 21:23. The people who sought His face will see it, Revelation 22:4, and the one thing David asked of the LORD is finally granted to all who are His: to dwell in the house of the LORD, not for the days of their life alone, but for ever.

sermon.title: Repose: The Power and Glory
sermon.why: Keller preached this sermon on Psalm 27:1-14 as part of the series The Prayer of Prayers: Exploring Jesus' Model, drawing out how the psalm's movement from confidence to urgent plea models genuine, Christ-shaped prayer.

quiz.q: What does David call the LORD in verse 1, and what effect does this have on his fear?

options.text: His light and his salvation, the stronghold of his life, removing the grounds for fear or dread.
options.note: David explicitly asks 'whom shall I fear' and 'whom shall I dread' on the basis of these titles for the LORD.

options.text: His judge, leading him to dread God's coming verdict.
options.note: The verse expresses confidence and removal of fear, not dread of judgment.

options.text: A helper among others, one source of confidence alongside his own strength.
options.note: Close, since God is indeed a helper, but the verse makes the LORD the sole ground of fearlessness, not merely one source of confidence among others.

options.text: His silent observer, giving no comfort at all.
options.note: The verse describes an active, comforting relationship, the opposite of silent, uninvolved observation.

quiz.q: What is the 'one thing' David asks of the LORD in verse 4?

options.text: To dwell in the house of the LORD all his days, gazing on His beauty and seeking Him in His temple.
options.note: This is David's single, focused, deepest desire above all others.

options.text: To defeat all his enemies in battle.
options.note: While enemies are mentioned, the singular request of verse 4 concerns dwelling with God, not military victory.

options.text: To receive great wealth and possessions.
options.note: The request is entirely about God's presence, not material gain.

options.text: To spend time in worship generally, wherever it happens to occur.
options.note: Close, since worship is central, but verse 4 specifically names dwelling in the LORD's house and temple, a particular place of God's presence, not worship in general.

quiz.q: What striking claim does David make in verse 10?

options.text: Even if his father and mother forsake him, the LORD will receive him.
options.note: This verse pictures God's care as more reliable than even the closest human family bonds.

options.text: His parents will never forsake him.
options.note: The verse is a hypothetical concession, 'though,' not a promise about his parents' behavior.

options.text: Human family will always ultimately be replaced by God's people.
options.note: Close in spirit, since God's reception is central, but the verse's specific point is God's personal reception of David himself, not a statement about replacing family with community.

options.text: He no longer needs any human relationships.
options.note: The verse addresses the worst case of abandonment, not a rejection of human relationships generally.

quiz.q: What does David ask for in verse 11, and why?

options.text: To be taught God's way and led on a level path, because of his oppressors.
options.note: David explicitly ties his request for guidance to the pressure of those opposing him.

options.text: To be given a new kingdom entirely.
options.note: The request is for guidance and a level path, not a new kingdom.

options.text: To have his oppressors immediately destroyed.
options.note: Close, since the oppressors are named as the reason for the request, but verse 11 specifically asks for guidance and a level path, not the immediate destruction of the oppressors.

options.text: To be left alone by God and others.
options.note: This is nearly the opposite of the request; David is asking for God's active teaching and leading, not solitude.

quiz.q: What is David's closing exhortation in verse 14?

options.text: To wait patiently for the LORD, being strong and courageous.
options.note: The psalm closes with a repeated call to patient, courageous waiting on the LORD.

options.text: To give up hope if deliverance does not come quickly.
options.note: The exhortation is the opposite, urging patient, courageous waiting rather than giving up.

options.text: To be strong on his own initiative, without reference to the LORD.
options.note: Close, since strength and courage are named, but verse 14 ties both explicitly to waiting for the LORD, not self-generated resolve.

options.text: To seek comfort in wealth instead of prayer.
options.note: The explicit exhortation concerns waiting on the LORD, not seeking comfort elsewhere.

questions: David calls the LORD his light and salvation, removing grounds for fear even facing an army. What circumstance in your life currently tempts you most toward fear, and how might naming God as your light change that?

David's one great request is simply to dwell in God's presence and gaze on His beauty. If you could ask God for only one thing, would it be this, and if not, what does that reveal about your deepest desires?

David's confidence in verses 1-6 gives way to urgent, almost desperate pleading by verse 7. Where in your own life do you need to bring bold trust and honest desperation to God together, rather than pretending only one is true?

David says the LORD will receive him even if his father and mother forsake him. Who or what have you relied on for security that could fail you, and how does knowing God's reception is more certain change that reliance?

The psalm ends by urging patient, courageous waiting on the LORD rather than giving up or taking control. What are you currently waiting on God for, and what would courageous patience look like this week?

translationNotes.note: Stronghold can also be rendered refuge, both pointing to a place of safety rather than merely strength.
Seek His face was likely a known call to worship or prayer; David's response turns the command into personal, wholehearted desire.
The land of the living can refer to this present earthly life or carry a broader hope beyond death, consistent with the Psalter's developing hope of resurrection.
